processing: Baked green: shoots are fired, rolled lightly, shaped slightly flat and dried gently with warm air, keeping the down and a fresh, un-roasted character.
harvest_season: Spring, from early April into May; the mountain gardens are high and cool so the main picking is around Grain Rain, with a smaller pre-Qingming crop from lower slopes.
appearance_dry: Slightly flattened, slim, lightly curved shoots in a greyish jade green with soft down.
appearance_wet: Even bud-and-leaf sets, tender and bright.
taste_profile: Crisp and sweet with fresh chestnut, a hint of orchid and a cool, mineral finish; lighter than Longjing but with a longer aftertaste.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan or glass at 80–85 °C. Mountain leaf: it stands a fourth steep where lowland bud teas fade.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, mostly from around Grain Rain for the high gardens; pre-Qingming lots exist from lower slopes and cost more. Production is small and mostly sold within Zhejiang. Drink within the year, kept cold and sealed.
description:
Tianmu Qing Ding is the green tea of Tianmu Mountain in Lin'an, west of Hangzhou, a high, forested range with old temples and ancient trees and a cooler, later spring than the West Lake hills an hour away. The name means 'green peak'. It is an old tea district that was nearly forgotten in the twentieth century and rebuilt from the 1980s, and today it is a small-production mountain green that locals prize and few outsiders have tasted.

It is a baked green made from the local seed-grown bushes: fired, lightly rolled, pressed only slightly flat and dried gently, so it sits between the flat Longjing style and the curled styles in look, and keeps a fresh rather than toasty character.

The cup is crisp and sweet, chestnut and a little orchid, with a cool, almost mineral finish that lasts longer than its light body suggests, the signature of high, cool gardens. It takes 80–85 °C in a gaiwan and gives four steeps, with the second the best. People who find Longjing too toasty and Mao Feng too soft tend to land here happily.

Because the mountain is high, the main harvest comes around Grain Rain in late April, and most of it is sold within Zhejiang as the current spring's tea. If you see 'Tianmu' tea in early March, it is from lower slopes or from somewhere else entirely. Ask for elevation and picking date, and expect the price to sit below Xihu Longjing and above everyday Zhejiang greens.

Lin'an is also the home of the Chinese hickory nut, and the local habit of taking this tea with roasted hickory nuts is worth copying with any toasted nut.
sources_note: No dedicated English Wikipedia article found. Revival 'from the 1980s' follows the usual Chinese account; exact dates vary by source.
